tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Links: [{"title":"Ghostty 1.3.0-arch2 segfaults on Linux/Wayland/Hyprland during long pi/AI terminal sessions (same crash offset twice) · ghostty-org/ghostty · Discussion #11504","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/11504"},{"title":"Default async-backend = epoll in Ghostty config causes SIGSEGV crash during burst writes (OSC color queries) · Issue #12917 · omacom/omarchy","url":"https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/issues/12917"},{"title":"Crash: OSC8 hyperlink hover during resize causes index-out-of-bounds panic in linkCells · ghostty-org/ghostty · Discussion #10032","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/10032"},{"title":"Crash during window resize while Python's rich.progress running · ghostty-org/ghostty · Discussion #8377","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/8377"},{"title":"OSC 133 does not parse key/value pairs with missing `=` properly. · Issue #10379 · ghostty-org/ghostty","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/issues/10379"},{"title":"ghostty crashes after lots of cursor movement and replacing text, then resizing window (contains debug log and repro file) · ghostty-org/ghostty · Discussion #7977","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/7977"},{"title":"Ghostty crashes when using a hyperlink · ghostty-org/ghostty · Discussion #4103","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/4103"},{"title":"Issue · ghostty-org/ghostty","url":"https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/issues/7499"},{"title":"Ghostty Release Notes - March 2026 Latest Updates - Releasebot","url":"https://releasebot.io/updates/ghostty"}]

Based on the web search results, I found several relevant GitHub issues and discussions related to Ghostty crashes involving null pointers and OSC hyperlinks:

## Key Findings:

**IO Thread Null Pointer Crash with OSC Hyperlinks:**
In ReleaseFast builds, an unreachable code path causes the IO thread to crash as a null-dereference SEGV, triggered by heavy OSC 8 hyperlinks during sessions with OSC title updates and synchronized output.

**Write Queue Callback Crash:**
Ghostty crashed with SIGSEGV in the io thread when the stream.WriteQueue drained q_inner during an earlier event, causing a subsequent callback to encounter q_inner.head == null.

**OSC8 Hyperlink Hover Crash:**
There's also a crash during OSC8 hyperlink hover mode, caused by an index-out-of-bounds panic in the linkCells function that indexes row_pins without validating bounds.

I found several relevant results about Ghostty crashes related to SIGSEGV issues, particularly in version 1.3.x. Here are the key findings:

## IO Thread Crashes with Heavy Output

There are reported crashes in the io thread triggered by long-running AI coding agents producing lots of streaming output on Linux/Wayland systems. A debug build revealed the root cause as an unreachable code path that in ReleaseFast becomes undefined behavior, causing the IO thread to crash as a null-deref SIGSEGV.

## Async Backend Issues

Ghostty crashed with SIGSEGV in the io thread when running TUIs that send bursts of OSC queries (such as palette color queries). The libxev epoll backend would encounter a null queue head during a subsequent callback in the same batch, causing an unwrap to produce NULL and dereference memory at offset 264.

## Fontconfig Thread-Safety Issues

Concurrent font discovery from multiple surface render threads can corrupt fontconfig's shared state, causing SIGSEGV inside FcFontSort, which occurs frequently during heavy output with multiple windows. A process-wide lock serializing all fontconfig calls eliminates the crash.

These issues appear to be known problems affecting version 1.3.x on Linux systems, particularly when running resource-intensive terminal applications.

content.content:
# Ghostty SIGSEGV Crash Summary

## Crash Mechanism
The crash occurs in `libxev`'s experimental `epoll` backend when handling write queue callbacks. The issue involves queue desynchronization: when `stream.WriteQueue` drains `q_inner` during one event, a subsequent callback in the same batch finds `q_inner.head == null`. The unwrap operation in `.ReleaseFast` dereferences a null pointer at offset 264, causing SIGSEGV.

## Trigger
Burst writes of OSC (Operating System Command) queries trigger the crash—specifically OSC 4 palette color queries sent by terminal user interfaces like `herdr`.

## Affected Versions
Ghostty 1.3.1 confirmed affected. The issue stems from the `epoll` backend's inherent instability under burst conditions.

## Recommended Fix
Remove `async-backend = epoll` from Omarchy's default Ghostty configuration. This setting was added as a workaround for Hyprland slowness but forces use of an "explicitly experimental" backend. Ghostty's default `io_uring` backend is fully supported on modern Arch kernels and does not exhibit this crash.

**Workaround**: Users can manually set `async-backend = io_uring` in their Ghostty config to immediately resolve the issue.

content.content:
# Ghostty Segfault Analysis

## Crash Signature
- **Thread**: `io`
- **Fault offset**: `ghostty + 0x1519bbd`
- **Version affected**: 1.3.0-arch2
- **Signal**: SIGSEGV at address 0x108

## Root Cause Identified

A maintainer (Jackman3005) using Claude Code traced the bug to a **capacity check mismatch in OSC 8 hyperlink handling**:

The `writeCell` function performs one combined capacity check for allocating URI + ID data, but `Hyperlink.dupe()` executes two separate allocations. Since the bitmap allocator rounds each allocation independently, two allocations can require more contiguous chunks than one combined allocation—causing the second `dupe` call to fail with `OutOfMemory` despite the capacity check passing.

The panic becomes a SIGSEGV in ReleaseFast builds due to undefined behavior from the "unreachable" assertion.

## Trigger Conditions
- Long-running AI coding sessions (pi, Claude Code)
- Heavy OSC 8 hyperlinks in output
- Column-count changes during reflow

## Fix Status
No specific version mentioned as resolving this. A collaborator suggested testing on 1.3.1+ or the debug build, but the discussion indicates "lots of work fixing crashes since" with recommendations to test the `main` branch.

**Note**: The discussion does not mention async-backend configuration (epoll vs io_uring) as relevant to this particular crash.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about this technical issue:

Ghostty crashed with SIGSEGV in the io thread (stream.WriteQueue.callback in libxev) when running TUIs that send bursts of OSC queries (e.g. OSC 4 palette colors). 

The root cause was identified: because stream.WriteQueue drained q_inner during an earlier event in the batch, a subsequent callback in the same tick encountered q_inner.head == null. In .ReleaseFast, q_inner.head.? unwrap produced NULL and dereferenced offset 264.

The technical explanation for this bug is that the epoll backend's dispatch loop invokes a completion's callback for every kernel event it receives, without checking that the completion is still outstanding. 

A fix was developed: libxev 34fa5087, stock vs. this patch, and ran the #234 reproducer (--config-default-files=false --async-backend=epoll -e bash repro.sh). This was addressed in Pull Request #239 of the libxev repository, which aimed to filter out stale completion callbacks in the epoll backend to prevent the null pointer dereference.

content.content:
# Analysis of PR #239

## Merge Status
The PR is **open** (not merged). The page shows "Open" status and indicates NonMirror wants to merge 1 commit into the main branch.

## What It Fixes
The PR addresses a critical bug in libxev's epoll backend where "the dispatch loop invokes a completion's callback for every epoll event without checking that the completion is still outstanding." This causes a null dereference when retired completions receive stale kernel events, particularly affecting queued write operations.

## Issue References
Yes, the PR explicitly references **issue #234**, which tracks a Ghostty 1.3.1 crash occurring on the IO thread at address `0x108`.

## Reproducer
The PR references a reproducer script but does not quote it directly. The testing section mentions running:

> `--config-default-files=false --async-backend=epoll -e bash repro.sh`

However, the actual script contents are not included in this GitHub page. The test results show the patch reduced SIGSEGV crashes from 6 failures in 14 stock runs to 0 failures in 13 patched runs.

content.text:
**Cause: your own `home.nix` line `async-backend = "epoll"` (home.nix:2970), hitting an open libxev bug that herdr's attach reliably triggers.**

### Evidence chain

1. **3 crashes today, identical signature.** All SIGSEGV in a thread named `io`, all at code offset `+0x146dddd`, all with `r14 = 0x0` faulting on `mov 0x108(%r14),%rcx` — a null deref at field offset **0x108 = 264**.
2. **Each crash is ~0.4s after a herdr client attach**, per `~/.config/herdr/herdr-server.log`: connected 11:07:32.30 / 16:27:35.79 / 17:03:28.37 → crash at 11:07:32 / 16:27:35 / 17:03:28. 3 for 3.
3. **herdr's attach preamble is a burst of 258 reply-generating queries.** I captured its real output: `OSC 10;?`, `OSC 11;?`, then `OSC 4;0;?` … `OSC 4;255;?` back-to-back in the first 1KB, plus `CSI 18t`, `CSI >7u`, `DECRQM`s.
4. **Upstream names exactly this**, including herdr by name: libxev's epoll dispatch invokes a completion's callback for every epoll event without checking the completion is still outstanding. `stream.WriteQueue` drains `q_inner` on an earlier event in the batch; a later callback in the same tick finds `q_inner.head == null`, and the `.?` unwrap in ReleaseFast yields NULL → deref at offset 264. Ghostty 1.3.1, epoll backend only.
5. **Your build confirms the backend**: `ghostty +show-config` → `async-backend = epoll`, and a test instance logs `libxev manual backend=epoll`.

The io thread dying takes the whole process down — that's why you lose every window, not just the herdr one.

### Honest gap

I did **not** reproduce it locally. 24 isolated runs of the upstream flood recipe (800 rounds of DA1/DA2/DSR/CPR/XTVERSION/kitty-kbd/`CSI 14t`/`CSI 18t`/OSC 10/11) under `--async-backend=epoll`, plus 4 real herdr attaches — zero crashes. It's a batching race; upstream measured ~6 in 14. So the mechanism is established from the crash signature, not from a repro I triggered. I made no code changes.

### The fix

The upstream fix is [mitchellh/libxev#239](https://github.com/mitchellh/libxev/pull/239), still **open** — so upgrading ghostty won't help yet. Your only lever is the backend:

```nix
# home.nix:2970
async-backend = "auto";   # or "io_uring"
```

The cost is the thing your comment block at home.nix:2938-2969 documents: io_uring parks threads in `io_cqring_wait()`, so ghostty shows up as `procs_blocked`/PSI iowait. That's **cosmetic accounting noise**. Trading it for "ghostty segfaults every time herdr attaches" is not a close call. `io_uring_disabled=0` on your 7.2.7 kernel, so `auto` will pick it.

### Next action (2 min)

Try it live before committing anything:

```
ghostty --gtk-single-instance=false --async-backend=io_uring -e herdr
```

Want me to make the home.nix change (flip to `auto`, amend the comment to record this crash as the reason, keep the NO_IOWAIT revert note) and run `hms`?

Sources: [omacom/omarchy#12917](https://github.com/omacom/omarchy/issues/12917), [mitchellh/libxev#239](https://github.com/mitchellh/libxev/pull/239), [mitchellh/libxev#234](https://github.com/mitchellh/libxev/issues/234), [ghostty#3224](https://github.com/ghostty-org/ghostty/discussions/3224)

        async-backend = "epoll";

new = '''        # `auto` picks io_uring on Linux. That costs the bogus iowait

        # `epoll`, which this was from 2026-08-28 to 2026-09-26, segfaults

        # and the `.?` unwrap in ReleaseFast yields NULL, which is then

        # so the whole process dies and every window goes with it.
        #

        # carries it yet. Re-test `epoll` once it lands; see also
        # omacom/omarchy#12917, which names herdr as the trigger.
        #

        # parks one thread per ring in io_cqring_wait(), which sleeps via
        # io_schedule() and so sets current->in_iowait. The kernel counts that
        # as blocked-on-IO -- it lands in procs_blocked and is flagged
        # TSK_IOWAIT for PSI -- even though the ring only holds idle
        # IORING_OP_POLL_ADD watches on the pty fds and no disk IO happens.
        #
        # Because every other thread in the cgroup is idle-sleeping, PSI's
        # "full" (all non-idle tasks stalled) reads ~100% for ghostty's scope
        # and sums up the cgroup chain into user.slice and /proc/pressure/io.
        # Measured 2026-08-28: fujiwara's session scope sat at full avg300=99.88
        # for its entire 88-day life with every disk at inflight=0; utsuho had
        # 4 rings, 4 threads in io_cqring_wait and procs_blocked exactly 4,
        # while Slack and Firefox read 0.00 (they use epoll).
        #
        # This is ghostty-org/ghostty#3246 / discussion#3224, whose accepted
        # answer was exactly the epoll setting. Kernel commit 7b72d661f1f2 (6.5)
        # gated iowait on having pending requests, which does NOT help here: the
        # armed pty polls *are* pending requests. The real upstream fix is
        # IORING_ENTER_NO_IOWAIT (kernel 6.15+, probed via IORING_FEAT_NO_IOWAIT),
        # which Zig's IoUring does not expose yet -- ziglang/zig#25566.
        #
        # So the accounting noise stays until libxev passes NO_IOWAIT. It is
        # cosmetic; the epoll crash was not.
        async-backend = "auto";
'''

assert s.count(old) == 1, 'anchor matched %d times' % s.count(old)
io.open(p, 'w', encoding='utf-8').write(s.replace(old, new))
print('patched')
PYEOF

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a

- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.

input.command:
git add home.nix && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
ghostty: back off async-backend = epoll, it segfaults the io thread

libxev's epoll backend runs a completion's callback for every epoll event
without checking the completion is still outstanding. Once stream.WriteQueue
has drained q_inner on an earlier event in the batch, a later callback in the
same tick finds q_inner.head == null; the `.?` unwrap in ReleaseFast yields
NULL and gets dereferenced at field offset 0x108. That kills ghostty's `io`
thread, so the process dies and takes every window with it.

herdr attaching sends 258 reply-generating queries in its first frame -- OSC
10/11 plus OSC 4;0..255 -- and took ghostty 1.3.1 down three times out of three
on 2026-09-26, each crash ~0.4s after the client handshake in herdr-server.log,
each core a null deref at 0x108 in a thread named `io`, all three at the same
code offset. The race is batch-timing dependent and did not reproduce locally
in 24 runs of the upstream flood, so the diagnosis rests on the signature.

mitchellh/libxev#239 fixes it and is unmerged, so no ghostty release carries it
yet; re-test epoll once it lands. See also omacom/omarchy#12917, which names
herdr as the trigger.

The io_uring iowait accounting this setting was working around (ghostty#3246 /
discussion#3224) is cosmetic and is kept in the comment. The crash was not.
EOF
git log --oneline -1
